findings.title: Team admin/owner check uses AND instead of OR, denying team admins
findings.body: The permission variable is named `isTeamAdminOrOwner` but is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. A user is almost never both an ADMIN and an OWNER of the same team, so this evaluates to false for ordinary team admins, and they are rejected with FORBIDDEN even though the intent (and the variable name) is to allow either role. Team admins therefore cannot add guests to their team's bookings.

findings.title: Calendar update uses the requester's credentials instead of the booking organizer's
findings.body: The handler builds the EventManager with `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — the credentials of whoever called the mutation. But the handler explicitly permits attendees and team admins to add guests, in which case `ctx.user` is not the organizer and likely has no calendar/video credential connected to the event. `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` will then fail or update the wrong calendar, so guests are added to the DB (and emails are sent) while the actual calendar event is never updated. The booking organizer's credentials (already included on `booking.user.credentials` in the query) should be used.

findings.title: No check on booking status allows adding guests to cancelled or past bookings
findings.body: The handler fetches the booking and performs the update without checking `booking.status` or whether the booking is in the past. Guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings, which will create attendee records and trigger `updateCalendarAttendees` plus notification emails for an event that no longer exists, confusing recipients and potentially re-adding them to a deleted calendar event.

findings.title: Guests array has no size limit
findings.body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` accepts an unbounded array. Combined with the fact that any attendee of a booking may call this endpoint, a single request can create hundreds of Attendee rows and trigger hundreds of outgoing emails (sendAddGuestsEmails emails every existing attendee plus every new guest), enabling mail-spam amplification and DB bloat. A reasonable `.max(...)` bound should be enforced.

findings.title: Email failures are swallowed with console.log, losing the error
findings.body: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` call is wrapped in try/catch that only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")` without logging the actual error or surfacing anything. Guests are already persisted and calendar invites updated at that point, so if email sending fails the new guests receive no invitation and there is no trace of why. At minimum the error object should be logged via the structured logger, and ideally the caller should be informed that emails failed.

findings.title: Duplicate-guest check is case-sensitive against existing attendees
findings.body: `uniqueGuests` filters with `guest === attendee.email`, a case-sensitive comparison. Emails differing only in case (e.g. `User@x.com` vs `user@x.com`) bypass the check and create a duplicate Attendee row for the same person, who then receives duplicate notifications. The blacklist comparison right below lowercases entries but the submitted guests are never lowercased, so `BLACKLISTED@x.com` also bypasses the blacklist. Normalize case on both sides before comparing.

findings.title: sendAddGuestsEmails receives the raw guest list instead of the filtered uniqueGuests
findings.body: After computing `uniqueGuests` (excluding already-registered attendees and blacklisted emails), the handler calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the original unfiltered input. Today this happens to be harmless because the email code only uses the list for an `includes` check against existing attendee emails, but any blacklisted or duplicate email that was intentionally filtered out of the DB write is still passed to the email layer; if that logic changes (e.g. to email the list directly), invitations would go to people who were never added. Pass `uniqueGuests`.
